title: Tidal announces ban on AI-generated music; 27 million tracks will be deleted
gist: Tidal will ban fully AI-generated music on December 9 and delete its 27 million AI-labeled tracks (6.3% of its catalog), after AI made up 43% of new uploads over 90 days and hit 60% on November 6; 96% of those tracks had zero plays. Detection will likely lean on watermarks (94% of its AI tracks came from Suno), but locally run and unwatermarked models make it a cat-and-mouse game, while Spotify, YouTube Music, Deezer and Apple Music still allow labeled AI music.

insights.claim: Over the past 90 days, 43 percent of new uploads to Tidal were fully AI-generated, peaking at 60 percent of new uploads on November 6, 2026.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Quantifies how fast generative AI content is swamping streaming upload pipelines.
insights.locator: Tidal debuted its initial AI policy

insights.claim: Tidal hosts 27 million AI-labeled tracks, 6.3 percent of its catalog, and 96 percent of them received zero plays in the past 90 days.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: AI tracks consume catalog and moderation costs while generating almost no listening; deletion is near-costless.
insights.locator: As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million

insights.claim: Tidal will ban fully AI-generated music and delete all AI-labeled tracks on December 9, 2026, escalating from its July 2026 policy of labeling and demonetizing them; music using AI tools with human elements remains allowed.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: A first-mover hard ban that could pressure other streamers or differentiate Tidal for artists.
insights.locator: As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million

insights.claim: Tidal says AI music harms human artists by misleading listeners and siphoning royalties, and has already removed about 66,000 tracks for impersonating artists.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Royalty dilution from AI uploads is a direct economic threat to the streaming royalty pool.
insights.locator: Some people don’t particularly mind AI music

insights.claim: 94 percent of AI songs on Tidal come from Suno, which added watermarking in 2026, and Google Lyria embeds SynthID labels, so Tidal will likely rely on watermark detection.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Watermarking by dominant generators makes platform-level enforcement feasible for most AI content.
insights.locator: Tidal hasn’t specified how it detects

insights.claim: Deezer claims a licensable AI music detector with a false-positive rate under 0.01 percent.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: AI-content detection is becoming a licensable product for streaming platforms.
insights.locator: Tidal hasn’t specified how it detects

insights.claim: Watermark-based bans will not catch everything because open music models can run locally on a GPU and some cloud providers skip watermarking, making detection a permanent cat-and-mouse game that will affect provenance verification across all media.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Provenance verification is an unsolved, recurring problem across media; tools in this space have long-term demand.
insights.quote: it’s always going to be a cat-and-mouse game
insights.locator: That will take care of most AI music

insights.claim: Spotify, YouTube Music, Deezer and Apple Music all still allow labeled AI music, though Spotify has removed millions of AI tracks based on user feedback.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Tidal's ban is an outlier; watch whether larger platforms follow.
